image.alt: A Philodendron Martianum in a white pot, its glossy paddle-shaped leaves held up on thick swollen stalks

light.label: Bright indirect light
light.note: Tolerates medium light, with slower growth

landscape_use.note: Frost-free zones, out of direct sun

snap: A compact, self-heading Philodendron with thick glossy paddle leaves held up on swollen, water-storing stalks — the reason the trade calls it the Fat Boy. It stays small, forgives a missed watering, and is toxic to cats and dogs if chewed.

deep_dive.title: Origin & Habit
deep_dive.body: Native to the Atlantic forest of southern Brazil, where it grows on trees and rocks rather than in the ground. It is self-heading, forming a slow, tidy rosette instead of climbing, and stays small enough for a table for years.

deep_dive.title: Key Care Rule
deep_dive.body: Water when the top inch of soil has dried, then leave it be. Those swollen stalks are a water store, which makes this one of the few Philodendrons that would rather be forgotten than kept damp — constantly wet soil rots it quickly.

deep_dive.title: Special Feature
deep_dive.body: The fat, inflated leaf stalks are the whole point of the plant. They thicken as it matures, so an established one looks like a cluster of green bottles holding its leaves up, and no other Philodendron in the shop looks remotely like it.

deep_dive.title: Pet Safety
deep_dive.body: Toxic to cats and dogs if chewed or swallowed; the calcium oxalate crystals irritate the mouth and stomach. Its low, table-height rosette sits within easy reach, so place it accordingly.
